query: measured cost of methods for For the class-matched detections in one capture, select_stage2_subset ranks that DetectionCandidate list with the strategy select_detection already implements. It applies that strategy by the first-maximum rule std::max_element already uses, so a tie keeps the earlier candidate and the later tied candidate stays deferred. It admits at most the count the caller passes, in that rank order, and places every candidate it does not admit into deferred, preserving their order in the candidate list. Each candidate keeps its source_index. Stage2Admission holds those two vectors, admitted and deferred. An empty candidate list returns both vectors empty, and an unknown strategy throws. The pose node calls it with its detection_selection strategy and a count of one, so stage 2 still estimates that single admitted pallet. The admitted source index and the deferred source indices are written on PalletPoseStamped after input_depth_stamp. The message already carries this pair's RGB and depth stamps, so the split is this capture while the scene can still change. When the estimate fails, publish no PalletPoseStamped and write the same two lists on the failure diagnostic, which is the only result that path publishes. The two early returns that publish nothing stay as they are. The user named which detections are sent through stage 2 versus marked deferred. The part they did not name is that the split is these two admission vectors, ordered by that first-maximum rule, on the pose result the handling process reads.
findings: The rank is one first-maximum pass, and that pass is not the frame budget. std::max_element uses exactly max(N-1, 0) comparisons and returns the first equivalent maximum, which is the tie that keeps the earlier candidate and leaves the later tied candidate deferred. On 1,048,576 ints, g++ 4.8.2 -O3 measured std::max_element at 0.989 ms and a hand-written scan at 0.293 ms. Arrays of at most 2,000 floats, 100,000 runs, took 2.670 s in GCC 11.2 for std::max_element, about 27 us a call. A scalar argmax over 32,000 logits measured 29.1 us, against 3.7 us for a NEON scan. A class-matched list is far smaller than those inputs. The pose node asks for a count of one, so admission is that single pass plus a second linear pass that copies every unselected candidate into deferred, in candidate-list order, keeping each source_index.

A full sort or nth_element is the measured alternative, and it does not build this split. On an Intel Xeon X5570 at 2.93 GHz with g++ 4.4.3, N=1000 took 8.2 us for nth_element, 43.8 us for partial_sort, and 111.4 us for nth_element plus qsort. At N=1,000,000 those times were 8.6 ms, 122.7 ms, and 83.1 ms. A full sort of the top 40 of 32,000 values measured 325 us against 18.8 us for partial_sort. Google's benchmarks put std::stable_sort 10-15% slower than std::sort, and it allocates a linear buffer. On one million random ints, std::sort averaged 107.8 ms and std::stable_sort 109.1 ms. nth_element partitions and does not keep the earlier tied candidate, and it does not leave the rejected tail in the original candidate order. The deferred vector is that original order, so the split stays the two linear passes. An empty candidate list is the N=0 case: zero comparisons, and both vectors stay empty.

Non-maximum suppression is a different selector, and its measured cost is an IoU pass that drops boxes. On a Ryzen 2600, YOLOv5 images took about 85 us with nms-simd, 0.21-0.27 ms with TensorFlow NMS, and about 72 ms with OpenCV cv2 NMS. The same machine's Faster R-CNN boxes took about 1.0-1.5 us with nms-simd and about 9 us with OpenCV. NMS returns the surviving indices. It does not admit at most the caller's count and place every other candidate in deferred in input order. A confidence or area first-max does not compute those overlaps. An unknown strategy is the throw path, not this scan.

What the count multiplies is the chamfer on each admitted box. Liu, Tuzel, Veeraraghavan, and Chellappa measured classic chamfer at 17.59 us per hypothesis and oriented chamfer at 51.50 us, averaged over templates of about 1,610 points; directional chamfer was 0.40 us. Classic chamfer on 1.05 million hypotheses took 0.42 s. One object's 3D pose was 0.71 s with directional chamfer, 29.1 s with classic chamfer, and 65.3 s with oriented chamfer. The pose node calls select_stage2_subset with a count of one, so that search runs on the single admitted pallet. Each deferred source index is not another hypothesis.

The same multiplier shows up when a second stage is paid per box, and it does not show up for a single-shot head. CosyPose spent 190 ms of a 320 ms scene posing every candidate (4 views, 6 detections per view, one coarse iteration and one refine iteration); association was 40 ms and scene refinement 90 ms. Faster R-CNN on a K40, VGG-16, measured region-wise time, including NMS, pooling, fully connected layers, and softmax, at 174 ms on Selective Search's roughly 2,000 proposals and 47 ms on 300 RPN proposals. Huang et al. cut Inception-ResNet Faster R-CNN from 300 proposals to 50 and reduced running time by a factor of 3 while keeping 96% of the 35.4% mAP; R-FCN saved little from fewer proposals because its box classifier runs once per image. EfficientPose says a detect-then-PnP runtime grows linearly with object count, while its single-shot phi=0 model stays nearly flat: 36.43 ms (27.45 FPS) for one object and 38.13 ms (26.22 FPS) on Occlusion images that typically hold eight. Deferring boxes saves a per-box chamfer or PnP. It does not shrink a constant-time head.

Both index lists on PalletPoseStamped stay in the flat part of the ROS 2 size curve. Kronauer et al. measured equal end-to-end latency at 128 B, 1 KB, and 10 KB; it rose at 100 KB and 500 KB, once UDP fragments past 64 KB. For a 128 B payload most of the time was DDS plus the rclcpp notification delay, and ROS 2 added up to 50% over raw DDS. One admitted source index and a short deferred sequence are a few integers beside the RGB and depth stamps already on that message. The handling process that already reads this pose gets the split in the same sample. The two early returns publish nothing, so they add no sample.

On estimate failure the same two lists ride the one diagnostic that path publishes, and no PalletPoseStamped is sent. REP-107 publishes DiagnosticArray on /diagnostics at 1 Hz by default, stores hardware-specific data as string KeyValue pairs, and says the channel is not a keepalive because aggregation can leave data stale. That 1 Hz period is the cost of the failure path's only result. The success path writes the same two admission vectors on the pose, inside the 128 B to 10 KB band where latency did not change.
